newsitem.title: USA: ITT Hartford posts $543 million loss after big charge.
newsitem.headline: ITT Hartford posts $543 million loss after big charge.

text.p: ITT Hartford Group Inc. said Friday it lost $543 million in the third quarter and took a $510 million charge to boost reserves for asbestos and environmental liabilities.

ITT Hartford, the insurance group spun off last year as part of the break-up of ITT Corp., said it lost $4.63 a share. In the third quarter of 1995, ITT Hartford earned $173 million, or $1.48 per share.

ITT Hartford said it took a total of $693 million in one-time charges, which included the $510 million increase for asbestos and environmental reserves. ITT Hartford said it has now boosted its reserves for asbestos and environmental liabilities to $2.1 billion.

The move, which had been expected, was the second major addition to the reserves in four years. In 1992, ITT Hartford added $594 million to asbestos and environmental reserves and $165 million for expected legal defence costs.
The latest addition was expected to resolve Hartford's environmental liability for the forseeable future, analysts said.
"This puts it behind them for the time being," said Standard & Poor's analyst Jonathan Godown.
Lehman Brothers analyst Peter Wade said the charge was larger than he expected, but should give the company one of the best reserves in the industry.
"Investors should be comfortable that the company won't be back to the trough for any reserve charges in the forseeable future," Wade said.
ITT Hartford said that, without the special charges, it would have earned $150 million, a 13 percent decline from the same quarter last year.

The company said its results also were hurt by an increase in the cost of catastrophic coverage. It said claims for catastrophic losses totalled $49 million, more than three times the year-ago level of $14 million.
Wade said that potential losses from catastrophes will keep earnings volatile and could put the insurer under increasing pressure to take steps to reduce exposure to catastrophes.

"The market is going to be less and less forgiving about it in future years," Wade said. As a result, he said, he believes Hartford will have to consider steps to reduce the earnings volatility, just as other major insurers have done in recent months.
Nationwide Insurance earlier this month said it would reduce sales of new property insurance policies in the coastal counties of 17 states to reduce its exposure to major catastrophes.
Allstate Corp. has taken a series of steps over the last year to reduce exposure to earthquakes in California and hurricanes on the East Coast.
But Godown said ITT Hartford's catastrophe exposure was not a major concern for the rating agency.

"I was fairly impressed with their catastrophe management programme," he said. Godown also noted that any drastic sales reduction in states like Florida could hurt the company's business with retirees.
With the special onetime charges out of the way, ITT Hartford must now show the ability to generate good earnings growth and good returns in an increasingly competitive industry.
"I think those issues are the ones that face the company in 1997," Wade said. "That's the challenge that lays in front of them."
